note: Wisconsin gives anyone receiving mental health or substance use treatment a statutory set of client rights, with a formal grievance procedure behind them and client rights staff who will write the grievance for you if you ask. That is separate from complaining about the clinician or the facility, and it is the channel most people in a Wisconsin program have never been told exists.

civil_injury.summary: Three years for assault, battery, false imprisonment and other intentional harm, and three years for negligence and other personal injury.
civil_injury.citation: Wis. Stat. § 893.57 (intentional torts); Wis. Stat. § 893.54(1m)(a) (injury to the person)
civil_injury.quote: An action to recover damages for libel, slander, assault, battery, invasion of privacy, false imprisonment or other intentional tort to the person shall be commenced within 3 years after the cause of action accrues or be barred.
civil_injury.note: 893.54(1m)(a): 'An action to recover damages for injuries to the person ... shall be commenced within 3 years or be barred' (https://docs.legis.wisconsin.gov/statutes/statutes/893/v/54). The 893.57 period was lengthened by 2009 Act 120 (per the section's history note). Claims against health care providers have their own rules, not researched here.

civil_minor_tolling.summary: For someone injured as a child, the deadline is the later of the normal three years from the injury or two years after turning 18, which is age 20. Wisconsin's longer deadline for childhood abuse (until age 35) covers sexual abuse only.
civil_minor_tolling.quote: (1) If a person entitled to bring an action is, at the time the cause of action accrues, either under the age of 18 years, except for actions against health care providers; or mentally ill, the action may be commenced within 2 years after the disability ceases
civil_minor_tolling.note: 893.16(2): "Subsection (1) does not shorten a period of limitation otherwise prescribed." The quoted text was read on the official page reached through the redirect from https://docs.legis.wisconsin.gov/document/statutes/893.16. Wisconsin is unusual: a minor does not get the full normal period after turning 18, only 2 years (or the normal period, if it ends later). § 893.587 (claims until age 35) covers only child sexual assault offenses (948.02, 948.025, 948.06, 948.085, 948.095, 895.442), not physical abuse under 948.03.

civil_government_claims.summary: For a county, city, school district or other local government, serve written notice within 120 days of the injury, and file an itemized claim. If the claim is denied, you have six months from the denial notice to sue. For a state employee, serve written notice on the Attorney General within 120 days of the injury.
civil_government_claims.citation: Wis. Stat. § 893.80(1d), (1g) (local governments); Wis. Stat. § 893.82(3) (state officers and employees)
civil_government_claims.quote: (a) Within 120 days after the happening of the event giving rise to the claim, written notice of the circumstances of the claim signed by the party, agent or attorney is served on the ... governmental subdivision or agency and on the officer, official, agent or employee
civil_government_claims.note: Under 893.80(1d)(a), a missed notice is excused if the entity had actual notice and there was no prejudice. 893.80(1g): 'No action on a claim ... may be brought after 6 months from the date of service of the notice of disallowance', and failure to act within 120 days counts as a disallowance. 893.82(3) requires notice to the attorney general 'within 120 days of the event causing the injury', and 893.82(2m) requires strict compliance (https://docs.legis.wisconsin.gov/statutes/statutes/893/viii/82).

criminal_child_abuse.summary: Physical abuse of a child can be charged until the victim turns 45 if it caused great bodily harm on purpose. Other physical child abuse, reckless abuse, failing to protect a child, and causing a child mental harm can be charged until the victim turns 26. The normal six years from the offense applies if it ends later.
criminal_child_abuse.citation: Wis. Stat. § 939.74(2)(c), (2)(cm); Wis. Stat. § 948.03 (physical abuse of a child); § 948.04 (causing mental harm to a child)
criminal_child_abuse.quote: (cm) A prosecution for violation of s. 948.03 (2) (b) or (c) , (3) , (4) , or (5) (a) 4. or 5. , 948.04 or 948.07 (5) or (6) shall be commenced before the victim reaches the age of 26 years or be barred
criminal_child_abuse.note: 939.74(2)(c) lists 948.03(2)(a) (intentionally causing great bodily harm to a child) and 948.03(5)(a)1.-3. (repeated physical abuse causing death or great bodily harm, or at least 2 violations of 948.03(2)(a)) among offenses that 'shall be commenced before the victim reaches the age of 45 years'. Sub. (2) begins 'Notwithstanding that the time limitation under sub. (1) has expired', so the general 6-year felony period still applies if it ends later. Offense grades were confirmed at https://docs.legis.wisconsin.gov/document/statutes/948.03.

criminal_felony_assault.summary: Six years from the offense for felony battery or assault. Misdemeanor battery: three years.
criminal_felony_assault.quote: (1) Except as provided in subs. (2) and (2d) and s. 946.88 (1) , prosecution for a felony must be commenced within 6 years and prosecution for a misdemeanor or for adultery within 3 years after the commission thereof.
criminal_felony_assault.note: Under 939.74(2d), DNA evidence can extend the period for felonies under ch. 940 and 948. First-degree intentional homicide and other listed offenses have no limit.

channels.name: Wisconsin Marriage and Family Therapy, Professional Counseling and Social Work Examining Board
channels.what_it_can_do: A combined board under the Department of Safety and Professional Services covering marriage and family therapists, professional counselors and social workers. DSPS provides the investigators and prosecutors for it, and the board disciplines the licence.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed marriage and family therapist, professional counselor or social worker in Wisconsin. Psychologists have their own examining board under the same department.
channels.how: File a written complaint through the Department's Division of Legal Services and Compliance. Board staff first decide whether it is within their jurisdiction.
channels.note: Complaints are accepted from clients, employers, colleagues and other agencies alike.

channels.name: Wisconsin client rights grievance procedure (DHS 94)
channels.what_it_can_do: Wisconsin law gives people receiving mental health, substance use or developmental disability services a set of client rights and a formal grievance procedure to enforce them. The provider must have a client rights specialist, and a grievance can be escalated beyond the provider.
channels.who_to_report: Someone in a Wisconsin program whose rights are being breached - restrictions, treatment, how they are being handled day to day - whether or not it amounts to abuse.
channels.how: File a formal grievance using the sample form, or ask a client rights staff member to write it down for you, which the Department says they will do. There is a published flow chart of the whole procedure.

channels.name: Wisconsin DHS, residential and community-based care licensing
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses and certifies Wisconsin's residential and community-based care providers and takes complaints against them.

channels.name: Disability Rights Wisconsin
channels.what_it_can_do: Wisconsin's Protection and Advocacy agency, with federal authority to investigate abuse and neglect of people with disabilities in facilities, a right of access to them, and free legal advocacy. The Department of Health Services names it directly as where to take a disability rights grievance.
channels.who_to_report: A Wisconsin program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.

channels.name: Wisconsin county Child Protective Services
channels.what_it_can_do: Starts a child protection response. Wisconsin's CPS is state-supervised but county-administered in 71 counties, and state-administered in Milwaukee, so the report goes to the county agency where the child is. An Access worker takes it and decides whether it meets the statutory definition.
channels.who_to_report: A child at a Wisconsin program. Anyone can report, to the local CPS agency or to law enforcement.
channels.how: Find the county agency in the Department's directory and call it; the directory also lists after-hours numbers. If the abuse is happening now or is violent, call 911.
